somalia.content: The Micro-Enterprise Trap: Why 98% of Somali Firms Are Untaxable - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Economy & Business Nationwide The Micro-Enterprise Trap: Why 98% of Somali Firms Are Untaxable November 7, 2026 6 min read MOGADISHU , The World Bank’s 2026 Public Finance Review paints a stark picture of Somalia’s private sector: the economy is overwhelmingly composed of micro-enterprises that are structurally almost impossible to tax, leaving the government with a revenue base that is narrow, fragile, and fundamentally at odds with the state’s ambitions. According to the Somalia Integrated Business Establishment Census cited in the report, 98 percent of firms are micro-sized, employing between one and nine workers. The census recorded 174,149 establishments, categorized as formal (28 percent), informal (25 percent), and micro-establishments (47 percent). Within the formal sector itself, micro firms represent about 97 percent of all formal firms, while small firms (10-49 employees) account for just 2.5 percent, and medium and large firms together represent less than 0.5 percent. This extreme firm-size distribution is not a minor statistical curiosity. It is the central constraint on Somalia’s domestic revenue mobilization. A tax system, whether it relies on income tax, corporate tax, or sales tax, requires taxpayers who keep records, who can be identified, and who can be audited. Somalia’s firm landscape offers almost none of those things. The Informal Economy and the Tax Base The report notes that the dominance of microenterprises, self-employment, and informal firms “severely limits the reach of wage withholding and self-assessment mechanisms among local private sector firms.” These structural conditions, the Bank concludes, “make PIT (Personal Income Tax) an inherently weak revenue handle and emphasize the limited scope for using the tax system to target redistributive outcomes.” Wholesale and retail trade accounts for 72 percent of all establishments, followed by public and social services at 12 percent, market-oriented services at 11 percent, and manufacturing at just 5 percent. The economy is concentrated in low-value-added services, where transactions are often cash-based, records are minimal, and the line between the business and the household is blurred. The 2025 Income Tax Law attempted to address this reality. It introduced a simplified regime for small businesses, replacing a complex corporate income tax with a flat 15 percent rate for firms with turnover exceeding $50,000, and a presumptive tax for those below that threshold. The presumptive tax is levied at the higher of $150 or 1.5 percent of turnover. But the report itself flags a concern: for taxpayers with sales less than $10,000 per year, the “higher of 1.5 percent or $150” formula “may lead to some concerns about regressivity.” In other words, the smallest businesses, the ones least able to pay, may face a higher effective tax burden than larger firms. As domestic revenue grows while external grants collapse , the pressure to extract more from this fragile base is intensifying, even as the base itself remains structurally resistant to formal taxation. The Parallel Taxation Problem The challenge is compounded by the fact that the Somali state is not the only entity taxing these micro-enterprises. Al-Shabaab operates a parallel “taxation” system that, according to UN estimates, generated approximately $163 million in 2019, equivalent to about 50 to 77 percent of the Federal Government’s domestic revenue. But those figures are contested. Guled Ahmed, author of Al-Shabaab Mafia Inc., argues that the UN’s long-standing estimate is a significant underestimate. Ahmed contends that Al-Shabaab’s yearly income peaked at approximately **$2.2 billion in 2022** and decreased to about **$1.65 billion in 2023**, a figure that would make the group’s revenue nearly seven times Somalia’s domestic revenue for that year. The Somali government, by contrast, claimed in early 2026 that a financial offensive had reduced the group’s revenue to less than $80 million in 2025. When the government introduced a 5 percent sales tax on electronic transactions in August 2024, Al-Shabaab moved aggressively to undermine it, warning banks against cooperation and targeting two markets in Mogadishu, destroying goods worth millions of dollars. The message was clear: the state’s attempt to expand its tax base would be met with violence. The 2025 Listening to Somalia Phone Survey, cited in the report, reveals the consequence of this environment. Nearly half of respondents reported paying no formal income tax. More than half said they would underpay taxes if they could avoid detection. Many viewed nonpayment as acceptable when government services are inadequate. But the survey also found a basis for hope: over three-quarters recognized the government’s right to tax, and a majority expressed willingness to pay more if revenues were transparently used to improve local services. The problem, the Bank suggests, is not that Somalis reject taxation in principle. It is that they do not trust the state to use their money well. The financial sector’s limitations reinforce the trap. As the IFC’s first investment in Somalia highlighted, fewer than 2 percent of businesses receive formal financing. Most micro-enterprises operate entirely outside the formal financial system, making them invisible to tax authorities and unable to access the credit they would need to grow into the small and medium firms that could be taxed more efficiently. Critical Note The World Bank’s data describes a trap. Somalia’s economy is composed of millions of tiny firms that are too small to tax efficiently, too informal to audit effectively, and too vulnerable to absorb a meaningful tax burden without being pushed out of business or into the hands of Al-Shabaab. The government needs revenue. The private sector, as it currently exists, cannot provide it at the scale required. The 2025 Income Tax Law is a reasonable attempt to adapt to this reality. The presumptive tax for small businesses, the simplified regime for firms below $50,000 in turnover, the flat rate for larger firms, these are the tools available when the tax base is a constellation of micro-enterprises rather than a concentrated formal sector. But the law cannot change the underlying structure of the economy. It can only work within it. The deeper problem is that Somalia’s tax base cannot be widened significantly without addressing the two forces that keep it narrow. The first is Al-Shabaab’s parallel ‘taxation’, which directly competes with the state and uses violence to enforce its claims. The second is the social contract, or rather its absence. Somalis are willing to pay taxes, the survey suggests, but only if they believe the money will be used to provide services. The government has not yet demonstrated that it can. The micro-enterprise trap is not a technical problem to be solved by a better tax law. It is a political and security problem. Until the state can offer protection, services, and accountability in return for taxation, and until it can assert its authority over the parallel taxation networks that compete with it, the revenue base will remain narrow. The 98 percent figure is not a description of the private sector. It is a description of the limits of the Somali state. somalia.content: Türkiye Allocates $400 Million to Space Program, Targets Lunar Landing and Somali Spaceport - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Technology & Innovation Nationwide Türkiye Allocates $400 Million to Space Program, Targets Lunar Landing and Somali Spaceport November 7, 2026 6 min read ANKARA , Türkiye plans to allocate more than 20 billion Turkish lira, approximately $398.7 million, to the Turkish Space Agency over the next three years, funding that will accelerate a lunar hard landing attempt in 2027 and the development of a spaceport in Somalia, according to the agency’s 2027-2029 budget. The annual allocation is expected to rise from $117.2 million in 2027 to $134.5 million in 2028, and reach $147.4 million in 2029. Of the total, approximately $398.5 million will support the National Space and Aviation Program, with a smaller allocation of roughly $533,400 for management and support. The funding is intended to reduce Türkiye’s dependence on foreign aerospace technology, support high-tech entrepreneurship, and finance research, development, and domestic production of space systems and subsystems. The Lunar Mission and the Somali Spaceport The budget’s most visible objective is the lunar exploration program. The spacecraft, developed under the leadership of the Space division of the Scientific and Technological Research Institution (TUBITAK), is designed to conduct research in lunar orbit and descend to the surface using a homegrown hybrid propulsion system. The target is a hard landing by next year, a milestone that would place Türkiye among a small group of states capable of reaching the Moon. The Somali spaceport is the other pillar of the program. Türkiye is working to secure independent access to orbit by developing domestically produced rocket technologies and establishing a launch facility in Somalia. As FTL Somalia reported on the $350 million facility in Warsheekh , the project was officially announced in December 2025, with construction beginning in late 2025 and the first phase expected to be completed by summer 2027. The site was chosen for its proximity to the equator, which reduces fuel requirements and improves payload capacity, and for its clear eastward trajectory over the Indian Ocean. The spaceport has drawn scrutiny for its dual-use potential. As FTL Somalia reported on the ambassador’s inspection of the construction site , French newspaper Le Monde has reported that the facility is designed to combine a satellite launch base with a testing site for long-range ballistic missiles, a claim that Turkish officials have not publicly addressed. The reported missile range of up to 2,000 kilometres would place large parts of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, and the Red Sea region within reach. The spaceport’s development has been accompanied by a visible military component. As FTL Somalia reported on the deployment of M48 and M60 Patton tanks to Mogadishu, the armour is intended to defend Turkish installations in the Warsheikh district, where the aerospace project is advancing. The tanks followed the earlier deployment of F-16 fighter aircraft to the area, signaling Ankara’s determination to protect its multi-billion-dollar investments. A Delegation on the Ground The scale of the project was underscored by a high-level visit in October. A delegation led by Fatih Dulkan, Deputy Head of the Turkish Space Agency, traveled to Mogadishu and Warsheikh for meetings and site inspections. As FTL Somalia reported on the delegation’s visit , it included representatives from Türkiye’s Ministry of Industry and Technology, the Ministry of Defence Industries, and Roketsan, the country’s leading defence and space technology company. The inclusion of Roketsan, Türkiye’s state-backed missile developer, reinforced the dual-use character of the facility. The visit came as Turkish officials framed the spaceport as a step toward “autonomous access to space,” reducing dependence on foreign launch providers and positioning Türkiye as the 13th country in the world with a sovereign space launch base. The spaceport is part of a broader expansion of Türkiye’s footprint in Somalia. Ankara operates its largest overseas military base, TURKSOM, in Mogadishu, where it has trained thousands of Somali soldiers since 2017. The two countries signed a defence and economic cooperation framework agreement in February 2024 that gave Türkiye responsibility for protecting Somalia’s maritime territory. Beyond security, Turkish firms manage Mogadishu’s port and airport, and Ankara has invested in hospitals, schools, and infrastructure. Somali officials have welcomed the spaceport as a milestone. Turkish Ambassador Alper Aktaş, speaking before his departure, said that “if I had said five or 10 years ago that one day Somalia would launch a satellite into space, many people might have laughed at us,” and noted that the project reflected wider changes in Somalia’s security and diplomatic standing. The first satellite launch from Somali soil is planned for 2027, with the Turksat 7A communications satellite identified as a potential candidate. Critical Note Türkiye’s space budget is a statement of intent. The $400 million allocation is substantial, and the lunar hard landing target is ambitious. The program reflects a genuine strategic vision: a middle power investing in the technologies that will define the next century, and doing so on its own terms. But the Somali spaceport is the weakest link in that vision. A launch facility in Somalia would require a level of security, infrastructure, and regulatory capacity that the country does not currently have. Türkiye has experience operating in difficult environments, and its partnership with Mogadishu is deep. But a spaceport is not a military base or a hospital. It requires a stable, long-term operating environment that Somalia’s current conditions cannot guarantee. The dual-use character of the facility adds another layer of risk. If the Warsheikh site is indeed intended for ballistic missile testing as well as satellite launches, Somalia is not merely hosting a civilian spaceport. It is hosting a military asset that places the country at the centre of regional strategic competition. The reported missile range would cover Somaliland, which has deepened its ties with Israel, and large parts of the Red Sea region. The tanks deployed to protect the site are a signal that Ankara understands the risks. They do not eliminate them. The spaceport also raises questions that the budget documents do not answer. Who will provide security for the facility? What agreement governs Türkiye’s use of Somali territory for launches? What benefits will Somalia receive beyond land leases and potential employment? These are not technical questions. They are political ones, and they will determine whether the spaceport moves from budget line to reality. Türkiye’s lunar mission may succeed. Its rocket program may produce a domestic launch capability. But the Somali spaceport, for all its strategic appeal, remains a project whose foundations have not yet been laid. The budget allocates the money. The security and the politics will determine whether the money is spent in Somalia or somewhere else. Hawadle clan chief issues sweeping call to arms against impending federal offensive in central Somalia November 7, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – The Hawadle clan chief on Friday issued a sweeping call to arms, urging members of his clan to take up arms in defence of their ancestral territory, honour and the Hiran region against what he described as rival clans exploiting the federal government’s name to advance their interests. Ugas Yusuf Ugas Hassan, speaking from his residence late on Friday night, called on all able-bodied Hawadle clansmen, as well as members of other clans in the Hiran region, to assemble at his home and mobilise against what he characterised as an imminent federal offensive. The appeal came amid reports that the federal government was preparing 1,500 troops stationed at the Hananbure military base in Galgadud region for an offensive intended to wrest control of Baladweyne from Hawadle clan militias, which seized the town just weeks ago. The militias have been mobilised by former National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) chief Abdullahi Mohamed Ali Sanbalolshe and other Hawadle politicians opposed to the federal government and the Hirshabelle regional administration. The political rift stems from President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s decision to endorse Ali Gudlawe, a member of his Abgal clan, for a second term as Hirshabelle state president under the ruling party’s banner. Hawadle politicians contend that the decision constitutes a repudiation of an earlier commitment by the president that a Hawadle politician would assume the state’s leadership in the next administration. Tensions in Hiran region have intensified over the past 48 hours following reports that Djiboutian forces, which control parts of Baladweyne, clandestinely facilitated the entry of Hirshabelle Vice-President Abditah Hussein Afrah into Baladweyne airport aboard a logistics aircraft. The move further inflamed the already volatile situation, with gunfire reportedly reverberating across the town throughout the night. On Saturday morning, some members of the federal security agencies appeared to heed the Hawadle leader’s appeal, defecting from the federal command and seizing control of Baladweyne airport. They vowed to bar any federal government or Hirshabelle official from landing at the airstrip. In his mobilisation appeal, the Hawadle Ugas called on members of the Somali National Army (SNA) belonging to his clan, including serving military personnel, to abandon their federal allegiance and heed his call to defend the clan’s dignity, the Hiran region and territories inhabited by the Hawadle against what he described as an impending military offensive. The appeal followed Sanbalolshe’s arrival in Baladweyne early in the day under heavy security protection from Ethiopian forces. Ethiopian troops were also sighted along the road connecting the border town of Ferfer to Baladweyne, providing security during his journey. Sanbalolshe had previously warned that, should Mogadishu launch an offensive against his clan, Somali army personnel belonging to the Hawadle would refuse to fight their fellow clansmen and would instead defect. Meanwhile, a mass mobilisation of militias continued in Baladweyne on Saturday, with heavily armed fighters gathering outside the Ugas’s residence, where he had summoned clansmen to assemble on Saturday morning. The mobilisation suggested that his call had been widely heeded. Videos circulating online also showed members of the security forces who had defected to join their clan. The Ugas appeared to invoke a supreme court ruling issued on Thursday, which declared that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud was no longer lawfully in office and that both his term extension and unilateral constitutional amendments were unlawful. On that basis, he urged Somali National Army personnel to reject orders from a leader he characterised as occupying the presidency unlawfully and without a legitimate mandate. He also issued a pointed warning to those who refused to heed his appeal, threatening that they would face the consequences. She indicated that this rapprochement may give the movement advanced combat capabilities. It also increases the risk of armed attacks targeting civilians and government forces in Somalia. Ali Mohamed Omar—a Minister of State at the Somali Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, known as “Ali Bal’ad”—stated in an interview with TRT World that the Houthis and Al-Shabaab differ in terms of ideology and principles. However, he noted that they do cooperate in technical and specialized areas. He warned that any support provided by the Yemeni group could contribute to enhancing the military capabilities of the Somali movement. The minister explained that Al-Shabaab does not possess extensive technical capabilities. However, the acquisition of advanced expertise in drones and weaponry could enhance the group’s ability to carry out more complex attacks—a development that threatens civilian lives and places greater security pressure on the Somali government. Ali Bal’ad noted that, for years, Yemen has served as one of the routes used to smuggle illicit arms into Somalia. He emphasized that these networks existed long before the emergence of the Houthi movement; however, they now raise further concerns, given reports suggesting that the relationship between the two sides has evolved from mere arms trafficking into technical and military cooperation. The Somali warnings coincide with a report issued in February 2026 by the Seldg research institute, based in the capital, Mogadishu. The report examines the nature of the relationship between the Houthis and Al-Shabaab, concluding that cooperation between the two sides has moved beyond initial logistical and intelligence coordination. According to the report, it now encompasses direct political, media, and military dimensions. Hussein Sheikh-Ali—the report’s author and a former national security advisor to the Somali president—stated in comments to *The Africa Report* magazine, published on February 17, that the relationship—previously limited to meeting mutual needs and arms trafficking—has become more organized and systematic. It has evolved into a pattern of cooperation that raises concerns regarding regional security. The report stated that communications between the two sides began with the exchange of information and the facilitation of maritime operations. These interactions subsequently evolved into logistical and technical cooperation. It noted that confidential sources informed the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen that the Houthis are providing training to members of Al-Shabaab on drone technology and the manufacture of both improvised and sophisticated explosive devices. Furthermore, a UN report issued in October 2025 highlighted concerns that the group might receive training to help it employ drones for carrying out attacks—a development that follows the group’s prior use of such technology for reconnaissance and surveillance missions.
